about_preview.title: About us
about_preview.lead: Each of us has a date that split the world in two.
about_preview.body_p1: Before 24 February 2022, our feeds were full of children's smiles, meetups with friends, and everyday concerns. Then came shock, panic, and an inability to grasp reality. But it was out of that paralysis that an unstoppable urge to act was born.
about_preview.body_p2: Within a few weeks the realisation set in: walking with placards was not enough. Inspired by Ukrainians in Melbourne, we decided to organise our own charity Sausage Sizzle at Bunnings. Our call for help was answered by the Ukrainian Women's Association of Australia (NSW), in the person of Mariyka Havryliv and Odarka — giving us official backing and the chance to act at scale.

hero.title: About the Community
hero.description_1: Our community in Australia is a reliable support base for Ukraine's defenders. The foundation's projects focus on rapidly meeting frontline needs — from tactical gear to critical medicine. We do everything to ensure every soldier feels supported, even from across the ocean.
hero.description_2: Here you can join fundraising campaigns, become a volunteer, and find like-minded people among thousands of Ukrainians in Australia. Together we turn every contribution into real help, build a strong community, and bring victory closer by acting according to our values.

story.title: Dreams: Our Beginning
story.ch1_text_a: If you scroll back through our Facebook page a few years, one thing becomes clear: our lives were divided sharply into "before" and "after" by a single date —
story.ch1_text_b: Before that date, the feed was full of happy photos: friends gathering, children smiling, jokes and everyday worries. And then — an abyss. Horror, panic, and an overwhelming sense of reality slipping away.
story.ch1_highlight: But from that shock, something else was born — something stronger: we must act!
story.ch2_title: First Steps: Martin Place and the Power of Unity
story.ch2_text_a: The first impulse came through the "Ukrainians in Sydney" group. When its leader, Anton Bogdanovich, called everyone to rally at Martin Place, we were there without hesitation. It was there, at protests in rain and sun, that our volunteer community was forged.
story.ch2_text_b: Ira Raevska and I had met earlier — our children swam together at the same pool. Now we were at rallies every day with prams. But after a few weeks came the realisation: just standing with signs wasn't enough.
story.ch2_highlight: We can and must do more.
story.ch3_text_a: Inspiration came from Melbourne. We learned that the local Bunnings network lets community groups run charity barbecues. We began searching for a supporting organisation, and the incredible women of the Ukrainian Women's Association of NSW — Mrs Mariyka Havryliv and Odarka — responded immediately.
story.ch3_text_b: became the day of our "baptism by fire" in Padstow. There was an incredible spirit! We all wore matching yellow-and-blue shirts, united by a common purpose. I remember a young man who was just walking by, asked what we were raising money for, and stayed with us all day to grill onions. Just like that. Because his heart told him to.
story.ch3_highlight: That day we raised the first $2,865 for a military hospital in Ukraine. It was our first big step.
story.ch4_text_a: We understood: support was needed not only financially for the front, but emotionally for those who had just arrived in Sydney fleeing the war. So in June 2022, our needlework circle was born.
story.ch4_text_b: It became a place of quiet therapy. Women who had been through hell and couldn't speak of it aloud would sit together, take up a needle, and as if "embroider" their pain into the fabric.
story.ch4_text_c: Those who had lived in Sydney longer brought threads and fabrics, shared warmth and tea. Together we preserved our culture, showcasing the beauty of Ukrainian embroidery at official city events.
story.ch5_text_a: Our second barbecue in Kirrawee in June set a record — $3,750!
story.ch5_text_b: But most importantly, that was when our volunteer family — lovingly called the "Tsybulky" (Onions) — began to take shape.
story.ch5_text_c: Why Onions? Simple: before every barbecue, we gather to chop mountains of onions. What used to be a "teary" solo task became a shared evening of jokes, support, and planning for the future.
story.ch5_highlight: Today we are not just a group of activists. We are a family that raises funds together for thermal imagers, body armour, and uniforms — bringing victory closer every day.
